findings.title: Permission check requires being both team admin AND team owner
findings.body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which means a regular team admin who is not also the team owner is rejected by the guard, and the request falls through to `isOrganizer`/`isAttendee`. For team bookings where the booking was assigned to another host, this incorrectly denies legitimate team admins from adding guests. The two role checks should be combined with `||` (or just call `isTeamAdmin`, which typically implies owner privileges) so team admins are allowed.

findings.title: Email comparison for dedup and blacklist is case-sensitive
findings.body: The dedup against existing attendees (`guest === attendee.email`) and the blacklist filter (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`) compare raw strings. Email local parts are conventionally treated as case-insensitive, so users can submit `User@Example.com` and bypass both checks even though `user@example.com` is already an attendee or blacklisted. All comparisons should lowercase both sides (the blacklist is already lowercased on parsing, but the input `guest` and the existing `attendee.email` are not).

findings.title: Calendar update runs with the caller's credentials, not the organizer's
findings.body: `EventManager` is constructed with `...user` and `credentials` obtained via `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (the logged-in user). When the caller is a team admin or an attendee (both of whom the permission check above allows), they typically don't have the host's calendar integration, so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` either fails outright or attempts the update under the wrong account. The organizer of the booking is already fetched at line 58; the manager should be built from that user's id/credentials so the calendar invite is actually pushed to the new guests.

findings.title: Emails are computed from the original `guests` list instead of the deduplicated one
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the raw input, but the DB write only used `uniqueGuests` (deduped against existing attendees and the blacklist). In `email-manager.ts`, attendees whose email appears in `newGuests` receive a fresh `AttendeeScheduledEmail`; this causes any email that was filtered out only as a duplicate of an existing attendee (e.g. an attendee resubmits their own email) to receive a duplicate booking-confirmation email as if they were just added. Pass `uniqueGuests` so the notification logic mirrors what was actually persisted.

findings.title: DB write is committed before calendar update with no transaction
findings.body: `prisma.booking.update(...)` (line 92) creates the attendee rows first, then `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is called separately, and only afterwards are the notification emails sent. If the calendar sync throws (e.g. bad credentials, see line 158) or the email send throws, the booking already has the new attendees persisted but no calendar invite went out; the client receives an error and the user is left in an inconsistent state where the API claims failure but guests are in the DB. Wrap the DB write and the external calls in a compensating/transactional pattern, or perform the calendar update first (with idempotency) and only persist attendees on success.

findings.title: Email-send errors are silently swallowed
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }`. The project uses a structured logger elsewhere (`logger` is already imported in this file); a plain `console.log` drops context, and swallowing the error means neither the caller nor an operator will notice that attendees were added but never notified. At minimum this should log via the project's `logger` (with `safeStringify` of the error) and ideally surface a non-fatal warning in the response.

findings.title: replyTo header exposes every attendee's email address
findings.body: `replyTo: [this.calEvent.organizer.email, ...this.calEvent.attendees.map(({ email }) => email)]` puts every attendee into the `Reply-To` header. Mail clients honor `Reply-To` and will deliver the response to every address listed there, so when the organizer (or any recipient) hits Reply, the message is broadcast to all attendees. The base `OrganizerScheduledEmail` only uses the organizer's email in `replyTo`; this template should do the same. Otherwise the organizer is one click away from leaking a private reply to the entire guest list.

findings.title: Newly added guests receive a generic booking confirmation, not a guest-added notice
findings.body: For attendees that match `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, the manager instantiates `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (the base class), whose subject/content is the standard 'Your booking is confirmed' wording. Existing attendees get `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` with subject `guests_added_event_type_subject`. The newly invited guest therefore sees a confirmation email phrased as if they had booked the event themselves, with no hint that they were added by someone else. Either reuse `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` (it already generates a `REQUEST` ICS method) or pass the `guests_added_event_type_subject`/`new_guests_added` keys down so the message matches the situation.

findings.title: Error toast prefixes the TRPC error code in front of the translated message
findings.body: On mutation error the toast is built as `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`. Error codes like `BAD_REQUEST`, `FORBIDDEN`, `NOT_FOUND` are leaked to end users alongside the translated message (e.g. 'BAD_REQUEST: Emails must be unique and valid'). Codes are an internal contract; show only `t(err.message)`, falling back to `t("unable_to_add_guests")` when the key is missing or untranslatable.

findings.title: Client-side validation reports generic 'unique and valid' even when emails clash with existing attendees
findings.body: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` only checks email syntax and mutual uniqueness of the typed list. It does not know about attendees already on the booking, so when the user types an email that is already a guest, the request is still sent and the server responds with `emails_must_be_unique_valid`, which the dialog surfaces verbatim even though the values were unique within the user's input. Either pre-filter the input against the booking's existing attendee emails in the dialog (the booking is already known at render time) or pick a more specific translation key on the server when the dedup against `booking.attendees` is what failed.

findings.title: Initial state is `[""]` so the form starts in an invalid state
findings.body: `useState<string[]>([""])` seeds the input with one empty email; pressing 'Add' immediately triggers `ZAddGuestsInputSchema.safeParse`, which fails on `z.string().email()` against `""`, surfacing the red 'emails must be unique and valid' banner before the user has typed anything. Initialize with `[]` (matching the empty-state branch of `MultiEmail`) or run validation only after the first onChange.

findings.title: Component mutates the `value` prop
findings.body: `value = value || []` reassigns the incoming prop before reading it. React props must be treated as immutable; this both violates React conventions and breaks if a parent passes a value of `null` vs `undefined` differently. Default-clone to a local `const` instead, e.g. `const values = value ?? [];`.

findings.title: Schema imposes no length bounds on the `guests` array
findings.body: `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` accepts `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `min`/`max`. A direct API caller can submit an arbitrarily large list (or an empty list that the handler then rejects with a generic error), enabling trivial abuse and unbounded cost from calendar/email fan-out on the server. Add a reasonable `.min(1).max(N)` (the existing dialog caps UI input to a small number) so the endpoint cannot be weaponised through a single request.

findings.title: New tRPC mutation ships without tests
findings.body: The PR adds a non-trivial mutation with a permission check, blacklist filtering, calendar sync, and email fan-out, but no test file is included. At least the following cases need coverage before merge: (1) team admin OR team owner is allowed, plain team member who is not the host is rejected; (2) emails matching an existing attendee (case-insensitively) are filtered out; (3) blacklisted emails are filtered out; (4) calendar failure does not leave the booking partially updated; (5) the new guests receive the guest-added email rather than a duplicate booking confirmation.
